subtopic: Deciding whether to report a cheating friend
subtype: Approach: reconsidering after seeing the friend's reasons [Revision]
passage: Right, I'm Nikita. When I confronted Joseph about copying, I had my speech about honesty ready. Then he snapped, “You don't know what it's like,” and I heard the rest: his father checks every mark on the sheet and won't speak for a day if it drops. That changed things, but not everything. I told him I understood the pressure, and that the copying still had to stop, because it wasn't fair to him or to the class. He looked at me as if I'd slapped him. Then I said, “What if we ask Mr Iyer about extra classes, and I come along?” We went on Thursday. Mr Iyer gave him a slot on Tuesdays and Fridays. My little brother says I'm the bossiest didi ever, but this wasn't bossing. The problem was never only cheating; it was fear.

qa.q: What does Joseph's father do when a mark drops?
qa.a: His father checks every mark on the sheet and won't speak for a day if it drops.

qa.q: How did Joseph feel when Nikita said the copying still had to stop?
qa.a: Joseph felt hurt and defensive, since he looked at her as if she had slapped him.
Joseph could talk to the school counsellor and, if he agrees, to his parents about the pressure he feels at home.

qa.q: How might Mr Iyer see Joseph asking for extra classes?
qa.a: Mr Iyer probably sees it as a good sign, a student wanting to learn instead of hiding, and he offers regular slots.

grounding: After learning the friend faced heavy pressure from home, a teen still insists on stopping the cheating but helps him ask for tutoring.
